To get a better prediction. That's what an ensemble is. An ensemble model is a predictive model that makes a prediction as a combination of several different predictive models. If you use the same type of models in multiple ways, it's a homogeneous ensemble. If you use different types of models, it's a heterogeneous ensemble. Often, it's more accurate than each of its single models. Why? Well, the general idea, just as in pub quizzes or team sports, is that two know more than one. This is not a perfectly correct assumption because it doesn't hold every time, but let's say that it does.

Based on our stacking model. So these are two general ways to combine multiple models. The second question is: how do we get all these models? We just have one set of training data. Well, one idea is bootstrap or bootstrap aggregating. We want to find multiple models that make different mistakes; the problem is that we only have one training set. So we can construct bootstrap replicates by sampling. You have your dataset, and you randomly sample new datasets based on the size of your original dataset, but with replacement. A strong learner is one where there's a possibility of having a high accuracy with a small add-on, so it will do very well. But strong learners are quite difficult to learn. Now, what does boosting do? Boosting uses a weak learner—easy models that aren't too heavy—and adds them to each other iteratively. The idea is you learn such a weak model and say: these predictions were good,

these predictions were bad; let's change the weights so that the next model you add will counter the first model.
